title: Aggregates, JOINs and Export to Excel

lesson.html:
By the end of Day 5 you should be able to:

  1. Summarize a whole table with COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX and ROUND.
  2. Give columns and tables short names with aliases (AS).
  3. Combine two or three tables with INNER JOIN … ON.
  4. Find "missing matches" (products never sold, branches without sales) with LEFT JOIN and IS NULL.
  5. Export a query result to CSV and import it into Excel with Data → From Text/CSV.
  6. Check that the totals in Excel match the totals in SQL.
  7. Work as a driver/navigator pair and keep a pair log. (Integrated: Lead small teams.)

lesson.h: Part 1 — Aggregate Functions: One Answer from Many Rows
lesson.html:
Sa simpleng salita: An aggregate squeezes many rows into one number, like counting all the receipts in a box, or adding up all their amounts. 500 sales go in, one answer comes out.

Function What it gives Example Result
COUNT(*) number of rows SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sales; 500
COUNT(column) number of rows where the column is not NULL SELECT COUNT(customer_id) FROM sales; 192
COUNT(DISTINCT column) number of different values SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id) FROM sales; 40
SUM(column) total SELECT SUM(total_amount) FROM sales; 49319.0
AVG(column) average (mean) SELECT AVG(total_amount) FROM sales; 98.638
MIN / MAX smallest / biggest SELECT MIN(unit_price), MAX(unit_price) FROM products; 12.0, 245.0
ROUND(x, 2) round to 2 decimals SELECT ROUND(AVG(total_amount), 2) FROM sales; 98.64

With WHERE: the filter runs first, then the aggregate.

SELECT SUM(total_amount) FROM sales WHERE payment_method = 'GCash';    -- 14253.0

Same as Excel! COUNT(*) ≈ =COUNTA(), SUM ≈ =SUM(), AVG ≈ =AVERAGE(), MIN/MAX ≈ =MIN()/=MAX(). And WHERE + SUM ≈ =SUMIF(). On Day 9 we will add GROUP BY to get one total per branch in a single query.

Sa simpleng salita: An alias is a nickname. AS total_revenue gives the answer column a readable heading. sales AS s lets you write s instead of sales, like calling Jose Protacio "Pepe".

SELECT SUM(total_amount) AS total_revenue FROM sales;        -- column alias: the heading becomes total_revenue
SELECT s.sale_id, s.total_amount FROM sales AS s;              -- table alias: s means sales
  • Use lower_case_with_underscores for column aliases (no spaces), so Excel and Power BI read them easily.
  • AS is optional (sales s also works), but writing it is clearer for beginners.

lesson.h: Part 3 — INNER JOIN: Combine Tables That Match
lesson.html:
Sa simpleng salita: The sales table only says "product 107". The name Argentina Corned Beef 150g is in the products table. A JOIN puts the two tables side by side and matches each sale to its product using the shared ID, like matching each receipt to the price list using the item code.

SELECT s.sale_id, s.sale_date, p.product_name, s.quantity, s.total_amount
FROM sales AS s
INNER JOIN products AS p ON s.product_id = p.product_id;
sale_id sale_date product_name quantity total_amount
TXN-10001 2026-01-05 Argentina Corned Beef 150g 2 84.0
TXN-10002 2026-01-05 Nissin Cup Noodles 2 56.0
TXN-10003 2026-01-05 Load - Globe/Smart P100 1 100.0

How to read it: "From sales (call it s), join products (call it p), where the sale's product_id equals the product's product_id."

Part Meaning
FROM sales AS s start from the sales table
INNER JOIN products AS p bring in the products table
ON s.product_id = p.product_id the matching rule: foreign key = primary key
p.product_name "the product_name column of p". The prefix tells SQL which table, because both tables can have a column with the same name

INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match on both sides. All 500 sales have a product, so you get 500 rows.

Three tables: the joined dataset

SELECT s.sale_id, s.sale_date, b.branch_name, p.product_name, p.category,
       s.quantity, s.unit_price, s.total_amount, s.payment_method
FROM sales AS s
INNER JOIN branches AS b ON s.branch_id = b.branch_id
INNER JOIN products AS p ON s.product_id = p.product_id
ORDER BY s.sale_id;

One JOIN … ON … per extra table. This gives a flat, readable table (500 rows, 9 columns), the kind Excel and Power BI love.

Join + WHERE + aggregate answers business questions:

-- total revenue of the Beverages category
SELECT SUM(s.total_amount) AS beverages_revenue
FROM sales AS s
INNER JOIN products AS p ON s.product_id = p.product_id
WHERE p.category = 'Beverages';                         -- 3244.0

lesson.h: Part 4 — LEFT JOIN: Find What Is Missing
lesson.html:
Sa simpleng salita: A LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table, even if it has no partner on the right. Where there is no partner, the right side is NULL (empty). It's like taking attendance: every student on the class list is shown, and the ones without a "present" mark are the absentees.

-- products that have never been sold
SELECT p.product_id, p.product_name
FROM products AS p                          -- LEFT table: keep ALL products
LEFT JOIN sales AS s ON p.product_id = s.product_id
WHERE s.sale_id IS NULL;                    -- no matching sale = never sold
product_id product_name
131 Kopiko Blanca Twin Pack
132 Spam Classic 340g
INNER JOIN LEFT JOIN
Keeps only rows that match on both sides all rows of the left table
No match row is dropped right-side columns are NULL
branches ⋈ sales 500 rows (Antipolo disappears) 501 rows (Antipolo appears once, with NULL sale)
Typical question "Show sales with their product names" "Which products/branches/customers have no sales?"

The left table is the one in FROM. FROM products LEFT JOIN sales keeps all products. FROM sales LEFT JOIN products keeps all sales, which is a different question.

lesson.h: Part 5 — Export to CSV and Import into Excel
lesson.html:
Sa simpleng salita: CSV (comma-separated values) is a plain text file where each row is one line and the values are separated by commas. Almost every program can read it, so it is the "common language" for moving data between SQL, Excel and Power BI.

Export from VS Code (SQLTools)

  1. Run the joined-dataset query (Q11).
  2. At the bottom of the result panel, click EXPORT → Save results as CSV.
  3. The Save As window opens in your lab folder (Day05_SQL_Lab). Type the file name Day05_Joined_Sales.csv → Export. All 500 rows are saved, even though the result panel shows only 50 rows per page.

Import into Excel

  1. Open a new blank workbook in Excel.
  2. Data → From Text/CSV (on the left of the Data tab).
  3. Choose Day05_Joined_Sales.csv → Import (on some PCs the button says Open).
  4. A preview window appears. Check that the columns are split correctly (Delimiter: Comma) → click Load.
  5. Excel creates a new sheet with a formatted Table (blue banded rows) of 500 rows.

Check: do Excel and SQL agree? (Integrated: Apply quality standards.) In empty cells beside the table:

Check Excel formula Must equal (SQL)
Number of rows =ROWS(Day05_Joined_Sales[sale_id]) 500 (Q1)
Total revenue =SUM(Day05_Joined_Sales[total_amount]) 49,319 (Q2)
GCash revenue =SUMIF(Day05_Joined_Sales[payment_method],"GCash",Day05_Joined_Sales[total_amount]) 14,253 (Q4)

If a number does not match, don't continue. Check that you exported the right query, and that Excel split the columns correctly.

Why not open the CSV by double-clicking? Double-clicking lets Excel guess the data types. It may turn codes like 0917… into numbers and drop the leading zero, or change dates. Data → From Text/CSV shows a preview first, so you stay in control.

lesson.h: Part 6 — Pair Programming *(Integrated: Lead small teams)*
lesson.html:
Sa simpleng salita: Two people, one computer. The driver types. The navigator reads the question, watches for mistakes, and thinks one step ahead. Switch roles every 2 queries.

Do Don't
Navigator reads the question aloud first Navigator grabs the mouse
Driver says what they are typing ("FROM sales AS s…") Driver types silently
Switch roles every 2 queries; record it in the pair log One person does everything
Disagree politely: "Let's run it and look at the row count" Argue without testing

Need Write
Count rows SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM sales;
Count different values COUNT(DISTINCT customer_id)
Total / average / smallest / biggest SUM(x) · ROUND(AVG(x), 2) · MIN(x) · MAX(x)
Column alias / table alias SUM(x) AS total · FROM sales AS s
Combine matching rows FROM sales AS s INNER JOIN products AS p ON s.product_id = p.product_id
Keep all of the left table FROM products AS p LEFT JOIN sales AS s ON p.product_id = s.product_id
Find "no match" … LEFT JOIN … WHERE s.sale_id IS NULL
Export Result panel → EXPORT → Save results as CSV
Import into Excel Data → From Text/CSV → Import (or Open) → Load

Term Formal definition Sa simpleng salita
Aggregate function A function that returns one value computed from many rows Pinagsama-samang sagot mula sa maraming row
Alias A temporary name for a column or table in a query Palayaw ng column o table
JOIN Combining rows of two tables using a related column Pagdugtong ng dalawang table
INNER JOIN Returns only the rows that have a match in both tables Yung may kapares lang
LEFT JOIN Returns all rows of the left table, with NULLs where the right table has no match Lahat ng nasa kaliwa, kahit walang kapares
Join condition (ON) The rule that says which rows match, usually FK = PK Ang batayan ng pagtutugma
Flat / joined dataset One table that already contains the related names and categories Isang buong table, handa na para sa Excel
CSV A text file of rows with comma-separated values Simpleng text na table
Export / import Saving data out of one program / bringing it into another Ilabas / ipasok ang data
Reconciliation Checking that totals from two tools or sources agree Pagtutugma ng total
Pair programming Two people working together on one computer as driver and navigator Dalawahang pag-code

• Aggregates turn many rows into one answer: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. WHERE runs first.
  • Aliases make queries shorter and headings clearer.
  • INNER JOIN = matched rows only. LEFT JOIN + IS NULL = find what is missing.
  • Export with CSV, import with Data → From Text/CSV, then check that the totals match.
  • Two heads are better than one. Drive, navigate, switch.

labTips: Type your query in the box under each question, then tap Run to see the result. Check runs every query again and marks it.
The word buttons (SELECT, FROM, WHERE…) type for you. Tap Tables to see every table and column; tap a name to insert it.
Any correct query passes: what counts is the RESULT (the same rows and values), not the exact spelling.
Every query runs on a fresh copy of the database, so you cannot break anything. Experiment!
Tap Check to see which answers are correct, then Submit to send your work to the trainer.
